title: Generosity that draws near
hookLine: a saying that measures generosity in distance: near Allah, near people

cards: Near, and far. That's the whole frame of a saying recorded by al-Tirmidhi.
In paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: the generous one is near to Allah, near to the Garden, near to people, and far from the Fire.
And the miser is far from Allah, far from the Garden, far from people, and near the Fire. Generosity isn't measured here in dollars. It's measured in distance: who you end up close to.

teach.b: Start with the people part, because it's the one you can test. Stinginess pushes people off. The friend who passes the dish first is easy to sit beside.
The saying claims the same holds with Allah. The Qur'an shows what this giving sounds like from inside.

In surah al-Insan, the righteous feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, and say, in Pickthall's translation: "We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you."
The gift isn't a loan of gratitude. Then Asma', the daughter of Abu Bakr. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, she came to the Prophet with a question.
She had nothing of her own, only what her husband al-Zubayr brought home. Could she give from that?
His answer: give, and don't count, or Allah will count against you. Don't hoard, or Allah will withhold from you.
That's the edge of this virtue: not a measured amount after checking the balance twice, but a hand a little more open than is comfortable.

And Bukhari keeps one more picture, in paraphrase: every morning two angels come down. One says: O Allah, give the one who spends something in its place. The other says: O Allah, bring loss to the one who holds back.
In the hadith, the giver isn't emptied; something comes back. So: give for Allah, not for thanks. Give without counting.
And, in the saying's own terms, the open hand ends up closer to Allah, and to people.

how: Muslims give through zakat, sadaqah and everyday hospitality, often recalling the hadith to give without counting and Qur'an 76:9, giving for the sake of Allah without wanting thanks.

games.q: what does “generosity that draws near” mean?
o: giving freely, which brings you near to Allah and to people
giving large sums so your name will be remembered
giving only to people who are already close family

games.q: generosity that draws near — tap the pairs.

s: the saying measures generosity by the amount given
it measures it in distance: near Allah, near the Garden, near people.
in al-Insan the givers ask for thanks
We wish for no reward nor thanks from you.
Asma' asked if she could give from what her husband brought home
give, and don't count, or Allah will count against you (Bukhari).

games.q: you're Asma'. you have nothing of your own, only what your husband brings home. you ask the Prophet whether you may give from it. what does he say?
o: give only what is yours alone.
games.why: give, and don't count, or Allah will count against you; don't hoard, or Allah will withhold from you (Bukhari).

practice: Open your hands on your knees, palms up, and notice how that feels compared to a closed fist.
Bring to mind one thing you could give, money, food, time, a compliment you've been holding back, and notice the moment your mind starts counting: is it enough, is it too much?
Let the counting go quiet and see yourself handing it over; if you pray, make the intention for the sake of Allah.

wordCard.voice: Generosity that draws near. Giving for Allah and not for thanks, without counting, so that the giver ends up near Allah and near people. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: generous, the word in the Tirmidhi saying.

carryVoice: Your line: near through giving. Measured in distance, not in dollars. Tomorrow, a quieter virtue.
